claims.text: The enhanced corrosion resistance of steels in chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments is primarily caused by a passivating surface or cladding layer.
The passivating surface or cladding layer acts as a barrier against chemical attack.
Standard alloy steel initially forms a natural, heterogeneous oxide layer.
The naturally formed heterogeneous oxide layer provides suboptimal corrosion protection.
Plasma treatment or chemical conversion coating can produce a uniform and adherent protective surface layer.
The engineered oxide or treated coating is chemically inert under the proposed exposure conditions.
A uniform and adherent engineered surface layer reduces diffusion of corrosive ions toward the steel substrate.
The engineered surface layer decreases the number of active corrosion sites.
The engineered surface layer limits ion-diffusion kinetics.
Decreasing active corrosion sites and limiting ion diffusion reduce the chemical-reaction rate at the underlying steel surface.
Coated steel samples will exhibit lower corrosion-related weight loss than untreated samples under the same conditions.
Coated steel samples will exhibit less pit-depth formation than untreated samples.
Coated steel samples will exhibit higher electrochemical impedance than untreated samples.
Untreated steel with a naturally formed inhomogeneous oxide layer will have a higher corrosion rate than coated steel under otherwise identical conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the coating retains its stability and adhesion.
The magnitude and durability of corrosion protection vary with treatment uniformity, steel microstructure, and exposure severity.
